Concerning the meaning derived from the first four verses of this surah, the commentators found it difficult to extract the meaning from its wording and arrangement. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) cites al-Wahidi in his *al-Tafsir al-Basit*, where he said: "This verse is among the most difficult in the Qur'an in its arrangement and its interpretation, and great scholars have floundered over it." Al-Fakhr said: "He did not clarify the nature of the difficulty in it. I say: the difficulty is that the structure of the verse is: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them clear evidence﴾ which is the Messenger ﷺ. Then God, exalted is He, did not mention what they would desist from, but it is known, since what is meant is the disbelief and polytheism they were upon. So the sense becomes: those who disbelieved were not going to desist from their disbelief until there came to them the clear evidence, which is the Messenger ﷺ. Furthermore, the word (ḥattā) indicates the endpoint of a duration, so this verse implies that they came to desist from their disbelief upon the arrival of the Messenger ﷺ. Then He said after that: ﴿Nor did those who were given the Scripture differ except after there had come to them clear evidence﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:4], and this implies that their disbelief increased upon the coming of the Messenger ﷺ. Thus, between the first verse and the second verse there appears to be a contradiction." End of al-Fakhr's words.

He means that the apparent reading is that His saying ﴿a messenger from God﴾ is an apposition (badal) to "clear evidence," and that the complement of "desisting" (munfakkīn) has been omitted because the context indicates it. For when the relative clause "those who disbelieved" was applied to them, it indicated that the meaning is that they were not desisting from their disbelief. The particle of endpoint implies that the coming of the clear evidence, explained as ﴿a messenger from God﴾, is the terminal point of their not desisting from their disbelief; that is, at the coming of the clear evidence they would be desisting from their disbelief. How then, when God says ﴿Nor did those who were given the Scripture differ except after there had come to them clear evidence﴾? Their division refers to their separation from Islam, which is an increase in disbelief, since it multiplies the doubts of error that prompt division in their religion despite their agreement on the root of disbelief. This last point is based on regarding His saying ﴿Nor did those who were given the Scripture differ﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:4], etc., as a statement connected to their aversion from Islam; and this is what the commentators have followed. We have a discussion on this which will come.

Among the aspects of the difficulty that al-Fakhr did not mention: observation shows that those who disbelieved did not desist from disbelief at any time, and the use of the present subjunctive after (ḥattā) indicates that it is governed by an elided (an) after (ḥattā), which implies that the coming of the clear evidence is future. This does not hold, since the clear evidence has been explained as ﴿a messenger from God﴾, and the coming of the Messenger occurred years before the revelation of these verses, while they continued in what they were upon: these upon their disbelief, and those upon their polytheism.

Now that the nature of the difficulty has been established, and it was presumed that it was in the mind of the commentators in general or in detail, it has become clear that this statement does not run according to what appears from its vocabulary or structure. It is therefore necessary to turn it away from its apparent sense, either by turning the structure of the report away from its apparent function, which is conveying to the addressee the predicative relation contained in the structure, by understanding the report to be used in a figurative meaning of the structure; or by turning some of its vocabulary, which the structure contains, away from the apparent sense of its meaning toward a figurative meaning or a metonymy (kināya).

Some commentators followed the method of turning the report away from its apparent sense, and others left the report in its apparent usage and followed the method of turning some of its words away from their apparent meanings. Among these latter, some interpreted the word (munfakkīn), some interpreted the meaning of (ḥattā), and some interpreted (rasūl), while some allowed two possibilities for "clear evidence."

The opinions of the commentators have multiplied, reaching about a dozen. Al-Alusi mentioned most of them, and al-Qurtubi mentioned most of them without attribution, and some of what al-Alusi mentioned overlaps, and one of them added what the other did not mention.

The sources for interpreting the verse return to five.

The first: interpreting the whole clause as a whole, such that the report comes to mean rebuke and wonder. To this view went al-Farra', Nifṭawayh, and al-Zamakhshari.

The second: interpreting the meaning of "munfakkīn" as going out from God's respite for them and their arrival at being called to account. This is from Ibn 'Atiyya.

The third: interpreting the complement of "munfakkīn" as: from disbelief, which is from 'Abd al-Jabbar; or from agreement upon disbelief, which is from al-Fakhr and Abu Hayyan; or: not desisting from bearing witness to the Messenger ﷺ as truthful before his mission, which is from Ibn Kaysan 'Abd al-Rahman, known as al-Asamm; or: not desisting from life, i.e., perishing, which is attributed to some lexicographers.

The fourth: interpreting (ḥattā) as meaning (inna) of connection, with the implied sense: "even if the clear evidence came to them."

The fifth: interpreting (rasūl) as a messenger from among the angels who recites to them scriptures from God. This is according to the meaning of His saying ﴿The People of the Scripture ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:153]. Al-Fakhr attributed this to Abu Muslim, and it requires turning the report toward mockery.

Furthermore, what is meant by ﴿those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture﴾ is that they disbelieved in the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, as in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were hypocrites say to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture﴾ [al-Hashr 59:11].

You do not lack the ability to trace the opinions of the commentators back to these fundamental positions, so we need not burden ourselves with mentioning them. Consult them if you wish. For our part, we should concern ourselves with interpreting the verse in its clear manner.

These verses came in the manner of establishing proof against those among the People of the Scripture who did not believe, and against the polytheists, showing that they evade the truth and make excuses for persisting in disbelief out of obstinacy. So we shall take the report in the manner of the place of proof, not the manner of conveying a predicative relation. It is therefore necessary for us to turn the structure away from the usage of its apparent sense toward a figurative usage, according to the method of the compound figurative metonymy (majāz mursal murakkab, a figurative usage in which the whole structure is used in a non-literal sense), of the type of using a report in the sense of an imperative or interrogative for rebuke and the like. Concerning this, al-Taftazani said in *al-Mutawwal*: that clarifying which type of figurative usage this is has not been addressed by anyone, while al-Sayyid al-Sharif undertook to clarify it in a way that leaves no doubt.

Thus this statement is presented in the manner of relating the strange and disordered opinions that indicate the instability of their holders' views. It is therefore a narration of what they used to promise, so it is a narration in meaning, as if it were said: "You used to say, 'We will not abandon what we are upon until there comes to us clear evidence.'" This is an indirect rebuke, in the style of a report used to express wonder or complaint about the obstinacy of the one spoken about. This is a rare and wonderful usage. Close to it is His saying: ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down concerning them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, "Mock on; indeed God will bring out what you fear"﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:64], where the form "fears" is used although they only displayed fear and were not truly fearful; and for this reason God said: ﴿Say, "Mock on"﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:64].

Thus the report is directed to every hearer, and its content is the statement: "There was a saying among the People of the Scripture, which was widespread among them, known of them, and established: the polytheists' excuse by means of it to the People of the Scripture when they call them to follow Judaism or Christianity, and they say: 'A messenger has not come to us as he came to you.'" God said: ﴿Lest you say: "The Scripture was only sent down upon two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study"﴾ [al-An'am 6:156], ﴿or lest you say: "If the Scripture had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than they"﴾ [al-An'am 6:157].

And the People of the Scripture's excuse by means of it when the Prophet ﷺ invited them to Islam is established. God said: ﴿those who said, "Indeed God has taken our covenant that we not believe a messenger until he brings us an offering which fire consumes"﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:183], and so on.

Its being widespread among both groups is an indication that the purpose of its context is to confound them with proof. For this reason, the expression with the present-future form in His saying ﴿until there comes to them clear evidence﴾ strikes the target, since they used to say this before the Messenger ﷺ came.

Similar to His saying concerning the People of the Scripture: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from God, confirming what was with them, and previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, yet when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:89].

The summarized meaning is: "You used to say, 'We will not abandon the religion we are upon until there comes to us clear evidence,' that is, the sign we were promised."

He made this a preparation and a preface to His saying after it: ﴿a messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures﴾, etc.

Now that the position of this verse has become clear and its difficulty has dispersed, let us move to the interpretation of the verse's words.

Al-infikāk (disengagement) is: ceasing. It is the reflexive form of *fakkahu*, when one separates and divides something, and it is used figuratively in the sense of desisting from something. The complement of "munfakkīn" is elided, indicated by the description of those spoken of with the relative clause "those who disbelieved," and the estimated sense is: "not desisting from their disbelief and not abandoning it," whether their disbelief was associating partners with God, like the disbelief of the polytheists, or disbelief in the Messenger ﷺ. This statement issues from the Jews who were in Medina and the villages around it, and the polytheists of Mecca who had not ceased to communicate with the People of the Scripture since the call to Islam appeared take it up, asking them for a clever stratagem by which they escape the blame of those who would reproach them for turning away from Islam. Likewise the polytheists around Medina from the Bedouins, such as Juhayna and Ghatafan, and some of the partisans in Mecca or Medina.

God related of the Jews that they said: ﴿Indeed God has taken our covenant that we not believe a messenger until he brings us an offering which fire consumes﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:183]; and He said concerning them: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from God, confirming what was with them, and previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, yet when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:89]. He related of the Christians, in His saying, as a report about Jesus: ﴿and a bearer of good tidings of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad. But when he came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is obvious magic"﴾ [al-Saff 61:6]. And He said concerning both groups: ﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could return you to disbelief after your belief, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:109]. He related of the polytheists in His saying: ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given like what Moses was given?"﴾ [al-Qasas 28:48], and their saying ﴿Let him bring us a sign just as the former messengers were sent﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:5].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 98, verse 1–3 (part 2 of 2):

There is no disagreement among the People of the Two Books that they were taken to covenant to await a prophet who would support the true religion. Its signs were set out as indications that would appear from his call, as in the words of the Torah in the Book of Deuteronomy: ("I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren, like unto thee, and I will put my words in his mouth"). Then its saying about him: ("But the prophet who shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who shall speak in the name of other gods, that prophet shall die. And if thou say in thine heart, How shall we know the word which the LORD hath not spoken? When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken") (Chapter 18). And the saying of the Gospel: ("And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever") i.e., his law, because the person of the prophet does not abide for ever ("Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him") (John, chapter 14, verse 16–17). And ("But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you") (John, chapter 14, verse 26).

And His saying: "And many false prophets shall arise, and shall deceive many" – i.e., after Jesus – "but he that shall endure unto the end" – i.e., remain until the ending of the world, and it is interpreted as the survival of his religion, since no one remains alive until the ending of the world – "the same shall be saved, and this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come" – i.e., the end of the world – (Matthew, chapter 24). That is, he is the Seal of the Messengers, as is clear.

The rabbis had misinterpreted the good tidings contained in their books concerning the Messenger who would follow, and they introduced signs by which they would recognize the promised Messenger ﷺ, which were fabricated illusions. Those who came after them remained waiting for those fabrications, and when they did not find them, they denied the one sent to them.

Al-bayyinah (the clear proof): the manifest argument and the sign of truthfulness. It is a noun transferred from an adjective, and it takes the feminine form because it is interpreted as "testimony" or "sign."

Perhaps the choice of this expression here is because it is the best rendering of the phrase found in the books of the People of the Book, which hovers around the meaning of "clear testimony" to every discerning person, as occurred in the Gospel of Matthew with the words ("for a witness unto all nations"). (Perhaps keeping this word here twice was for this particularity.) It was also mentioned alongside the earlier scriptures in His saying: ﴿And they say, "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?" Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133].

The apparent view is that the definite article in al-bayyinah is the "mental-knowledge" definite (al-'ahd al-dhihni), which is when what is meant is something known by its type rather than by its individual, as in their saying: "Enter the market," not meaning a specific market but whatever has the reality of a market. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"And war is only what you have known and tasted."

For this reason the scholars of rhetoric said: the noun defined by this alif-lam is in meaning indefinite; so it is as if it were said: "until there comes to them a clear proof."

It is also possible that the definiteness refers to something known to those being spoken of; i.e., the clear proof which is the bequests of their prophets, which is known to each group among them, even though they differed in imagining it and went far in their conjecture with what their fancies and fabrications dictated to them.

The word al-bayyinah was chosen because it expresses the meaning found in their discourse, and therefore we see its root repeated in many verses of the Qur'an on this theme, as in His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133]; and His saying: ﴿Then when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is clear magic."﴾ [al-Saff: 6]; and His saying: ﴿after the truth had become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109]; and He said of the Qur'an: ﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

The "min" in His saying "from the People of the Book" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), explaining "those who disbelieved."

He placed the People of the Book before the polytheists here, although the disbelief of the polytheists is more severe than that of the People of the Book, because the People of the Book have precedence in this matter: they are the ones who spread among the polytheists the notion that the described clear proof applies to them, and so they supported the polytheists in denying the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ with what was more solid than the trivialities of the polytheists, since the polytheists were unlettered and knew nothing of the circumstances of the messengers and the laws. When the Muhammadan call shook them, they turned to the Jews to receive from them what they could use to repel that call, especially after the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Medina.

So the primary aim of the refutation is the claim of the People of the Book, while the polytheists follow them.

Know that it is possible that the speech ends at His saying ﴿until there comes to them the clear proof﴾, so the pause is there, and His saying ﴿a messenger from God﴾ to the end is a new sentence in explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), and this is the view of al-Farra', i.e., "he is a messenger from God," meaning: because the ambiguity in "the clear proof" arouses the question of an inquirer about the description of this clear proof. It is a parenthetical clause between the sentence ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist﴾ to the end, and between the sentence ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear proof had come to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 4].

It is also possible that "a messenger" is an appositive to "the clear proof," so that it is a complete part of the expression "clear proof," and thus it is a report of what they claimed. The aim is to refute their excuses and to establish the proof against them, that the clear proof they were awaiting has arrived, but they do not reflect, or do not act fairly, or do not understand. God the Exalted said: ﴿But when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89].

The indefiniteness of "a messenger" is for the category intended by it, to ease what is difficult, like the indefinite in His exalted saying: ﴿for a specified number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184] and the saying ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. A Book sent down to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 1].

In this clarification there is a refutation of their excuses, as if it were said: "Then the clear proof has come to you," in the manner of His exalted saying: ﴿Lest you say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner." But there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19]. And this indicates that the clear proof is the Messenger.

The style of this response is like the style of His exalted saying: ﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause to gush forth for us from the earth a spring"﴾ [al-Isra': 90] ﴿Or you will have a garden of palms and grapes and cause rivers to gush forth within it in force﴾ [al-Isra': 91] ﴿Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments, as you claimed, or you bring God and the angels as a guarantee﴾ [al-Isra': 92] ﴿Or you have a house of gold or ascend into the sky. And we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book we can read." Say, "Exalted is my Lord! Was I but a human messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra': 93] ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said, "Has God sent a human as a messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra': 94].

In this there is a reminder of their error, for their books promised only the coming of a messenger with a law and a book confirming what was before him, and this falls within the saying of the Torah ("and I will put my words in his mouth").

And the saying of the Gospel ("and he will remind you of all that I have told you"), as has passed just above, and this is what His exalted saying indicated: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48], because the Torah and the Gospel described the promised prophet only as being like Moses or like Jesus, i.e., in that he is a messenger to whom God reveals a law, who conveys from God and speaks by His revelation, and whose sign is truthfulness, as has passed just above. The Proof of Islam (Hujjat al-Islam) said in al-Munqidh min al-Dalal: "The totality of virtuous character in our Prophet reached the point of miracle, and his miracles were extreme in their manifestness and abundance."

"From God" is connected to "a messenger," and he did not take the form of an annexation (idafah) so that the tanwin of "a messenger" could be realized, which conveys the magnification of this Messenger.

The clause ﴿reciting purified pages﴾ etc. is a second adjective or a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is an inclusion (idmaj) in praise of the Qur'an, since the apparent point is that the Messenger promised in their books was not described as reciting purified pages.

Recitation (al-tilawah) is repeating speech without adding to it or subtracting from it, whether it is written speech or memorized by heart. So the verb yatlu indicates that he reads to them speech whose words are not altered, which is the revelation sent down to him.

The suhuf (pages): the sheets and parchments prepared to be written upon, which may be of parchment or skin, or of rags. Calling what the Messenger recites "pages" is a metaphor by the relation of what will be (majaz bi-'alaqat al-ayulah), since he is commanded to write it down, so when he recites it, it will be pages. This metaphor is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf: 36]. This is an indication that God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to write the Qur'an on pages and on what resembles pages, such as shoulder-blades of sheep, rags, and stones, and that the revelation sent down to the Messenger was called a Book in His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51], for this very meaning.

The transitive use of the verb yatlu to suhuf is a well-known metonymic metaphor (majaz mursal) which has become equal to the literal sense. God the Exalted said: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48]; it is in view of the recited thing being written. The Messenger ﷺ used to recite the Qur'an to them from memory and did not read it from pages, so the meaning of "reciting pages" is reciting what is written in pages, and the indication is clear, namely the well-known fact that he ﷺ was unlettered.

The pages are described as "purified" (mutahharah), a derivative from the metaphorical purity, i.e., that its meanings have no confusion and do not contain anything misleading. This is an allusion to some of what is in the hands of the People of the Book of distortion and fancies.

The pages which the Messenger of God ﷺ recites are described as containing books, and books: the plural of kitab, which is a noun (fi'al) in the sense of "what is written." The meaning of the books being in the pages is that the pages on which the Qur'an is written contain the Qur'an, and it contains what the books of the earlier messengers included, of what is pure of distortion and falsehood. This is as God the Exalted said: ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97], and He said: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former pages﴾ [al-A'la: 18] ﴿the pages of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 19]. The Qur'an is the essence of what is in the earlier books and the collection of their fruit, so the name "books" was applied to the fruit of the books by way of the metaphor of part (majaz al-juz'iyyah).

By "the books" is meant the parts of the Qur'an or its surahs, which are in the position of books.

Al-qayyimah: the upright, i.e., firmly standing, where standing is here a metaphor for perfection and correctness; this is from representing the intelligible by the sensible, likening it to the one standing for its readiness for beneficial action. Its opposite is crookedness, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Praise be to God, who has sent down upon His servant the Book and has not made in it any crookedness, but made it straight﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], i.e., He did not place in it the deficiency of falsehood and error. So qayyimah is an intensive form of the one who stands, like sayyid for sa'id and mayyit.

The feminine form of the adjective is in consideration of its being an adjective for a plural.

Furthermore, what is meant by ﴿those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture﴾ is that they disbelieved in the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, as in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen those who were hypocrites say to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture﴾ [al-Hashr 59:11].

You do not lack the ability to trace the opinions of the commentators back to these fundamental positions, so we need not burden ourselves with mentioning them. Consult them if you wish. For our part, we should concern ourselves with interpreting the verse in its clear manner.

These verses came in the manner of establishing proof against those among the People of the Scripture who did not believe, and against the polytheists, showing that they evade the truth and make excuses for persisting in disbelief out of obstinacy. So we shall take the report in the manner of the place of proof, not the manner of conveying a predicative relation. It is therefore necessary for us to turn the structure away from the usage of its apparent sense toward a figurative usage, according to the method of the compound figurative metonymy (majāz mursal murakkab, a figurative usage in which the whole structure is used in a non-literal sense), of the type of using a report in the sense of an imperative or interrogative for rebuke and the like. Concerning this, al-Taftazani said in *al-Mutawwal*: that clarifying which type of figurative usage this is has not been addressed by anyone, while al-Sayyid al-Sharif undertook to clarify it in a way that leaves no doubt.

Thus this statement is presented in the manner of relating the strange and disordered opinions that indicate the instability of their holders' views. It is therefore a narration of what they used to promise, so it is a narration in meaning, as if it were said: "You used to say, 'We will not abandon what we are upon until there comes to us clear evidence.'" This is an indirect rebuke, in the style of a report used to express wonder or complaint about the obstinacy of the one spoken about. This is a rare and wonderful usage. Close to it is His saying: ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down concerning them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, "Mock on; indeed God will bring out what you fear"﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:64], where the form "fears" is used although they only displayed fear and were not truly fearful; and for this reason God said: ﴿Say, "Mock on"﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:64].

Thus the report is directed to every hearer, and its content is the statement: "There was a saying among the People of the Scripture, which was widespread among them, known of them, and established: the polytheists' excuse by means of it to the People of the Scripture when they call them to follow Judaism or Christianity, and they say: 'A messenger has not come to us as he came to you.'" Its being widespread among both groups is an indication that the purpose of its context is to confound them with proof. For this reason, the expression with the present-future form in His saying ﴿until there comes to them clear evidence﴾ strikes the target, since they used to say this before the Messenger ﷺ came.

Similar to His saying concerning the People of the Scripture: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from God, confirming what was with them, and previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, yet when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:89].

The summarized meaning is: "You used to say, 'We will not abandon the religion we are upon until there comes to us clear evidence,' that is, the sign we were promised."

He made this a preparation and a preface to His saying after it: ﴿a messenger from God, reciting purified scriptures﴾, etc.

Now that the position of this verse has become clear and its difficulty has dispersed, let us move to the interpretation of the verse's words.

Al-infikāk (disengagement) is: ceasing. It is the reflexive form of *fakkahu*, when one separates and divides something, and it is used figuratively in the sense of desisting from something. This statement issues from the Jews who were in Medina and the villages around it, and the polytheists of Mecca who had not ceased to communicate with the People of the Scripture since the call to Islam appeared take it up, asking them for a clever stratagem by which they escape the blame of those who would reproach them for turning away from Islam. Likewise the polytheists around Medina from the Bedouins, such as Juhayna and Ghatafan, and some of the partisans in Mecca or Medina.

God related of the Jews that they said: ﴿Indeed God has taken our covenant that we not believe a messenger until he brings us an offering which fire consumes﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:183]; and He said concerning them: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from God, confirming what was with them, and previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, yet when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:89]. But when he came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is obvious magic"﴾ [al-Saff 61:6]. And He said concerning both groups: ﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could return you to disbelief after your belief, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:109]. He related of the polytheists in His saying: ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given like what Moses was given?"﴾ [al-Qasas 28:48], and their saying ﴿Let him bring us a sign just as the former messengers were sent﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:5].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 98, verse 1–3 (part 2 of 2):

There is no disagreement among the People of the Two Books that they were taken to covenant to await a prophet who would support the true religion. Its signs were set out as indications that would appear from his call, as in the words of the Torah in the Book of Deuteronomy: ("I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren, like unto thee, and I will put my words in his mouth"). Then its saying about him: ("But the prophet who shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who shall speak in the name of other gods, that prophet shall die. And the saying of the Gospel: ("And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever") i.e., his law, because the person of the prophet does not abide for ever ("Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him") (John, chapter 14, verse 16–17). And ("But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you") (John, chapter 14, verse 26).

And His saying: "And many false prophets shall arise, and shall deceive many" – i.e., after Jesus – "but he that shall endure unto the end" – i.e., remain until the ending of the world, and it is interpreted as the survival of his religion, since no one remains alive until the ending of the world – "the same shall be saved, and this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come" – i.e., the end of the world – (Matthew, chapter 24). The rabbis had misinterpreted the good tidings contained in their books concerning the Messenger who would follow, and they introduced signs by which they would recognize the promised Messenger ﷺ, which were fabricated illusions. Those who came after them remained waiting for those fabrications, and when they did not find them, they denied the one sent to them.

From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

For this reason the scholars of rhetoric said: the noun defined by this alif-lam is in meaning indefinite; so it is as if it were said: "until there comes to them a clear proof."

It is also possible that the definiteness refers to something known to those being spoken of; i.e., the clear proof which is the bequests of their prophets, which is known to each group among them, even though they differed in imagining it and went far in their conjecture with what their fancies and fabrications dictated to them.

The word al-bayyinah was chosen because it expresses the meaning found in their discourse, and therefore we see its root repeated in many verses of the Qur'an on this theme, as in His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133]; and His saying: ﴿Then when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is clear magic."﴾ [al-Saff: 6]; and His saying: ﴿after the truth had become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109]; and He said of the Qur'an: ﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

He placed the People of the Book before the polytheists here, although the disbelief of the polytheists is more severe than that of the People of the Book, because the People of the Book have precedence in this matter: they are the ones who spread among the polytheists the notion that the described clear proof applies to them, and so they supported the polytheists in denying the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ with what was more solid than the trivialities of the polytheists, since the polytheists were unlettered and knew nothing of the circumstances of the messengers and the laws. When the Muhammadan call shook them, they turned to the Jews to receive from them what they could use to repel that call, especially after the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Medina.

So the primary aim of the refutation is the claim of the People of the Book, while the polytheists follow them.

The aim is to refute their excuses and to establish the proof against them, that the clear proof they were awaiting has arrived, but they do not reflect, or do not act fairly, or do not understand. The Proof of Islam (Hujjat al-Islam) said in al-Munqidh min al-Dalal: "The totality of virtuous character in our Prophet reached the point of miracle, and his miracles were extreme in their manifestness and abundance."

"From God" is connected to "a messenger," and he did not take the form of an annexation (idafah) so that the tanwin of "a messenger" could be realized, which conveys the magnification of this Messenger.

The clause ﴿reciting purified pages﴾ etc. is a second adjective or a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is an inclusion (idmaj) in praise of the Qur'an, since the apparent point is that the Messenger promised in their books was not described as reciting purified pages.

Recitation (al-tilawah) is repeating speech without adding to it or subtracting from it, whether it is written speech or memorized by heart. So the verb yatlu indicates that he reads to them speech whose words are not altered, which is the revelation sent down to him.

The suhuf (pages): the sheets and parchments prepared to be written upon, which may be of parchment or skin, or of rags. Calling what the Messenger recites "pages" is a metaphor by the relation of what will be (majaz bi-'alaqat al-ayulah), since he is commanded to write it down, so when he recites it, it will be pages. This metaphor is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf: 36]. This is an indication that God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to write the Qur'an on pages and on what resembles pages, such as shoulder-blades of sheep, rags, and stones, and that the revelation sent down to the Messenger was called a Book in His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51], for this very meaning.

The transitive use of the verb yatlu to suhuf is a well-known metonymic metaphor (majaz mursal) which has become equal to the literal sense. God the Exalted said: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48]; it is in view of the recited thing being written. The Messenger ﷺ used to recite the Qur'an to them from memory and did not read it from pages, so the meaning of "reciting pages" is reciting what is written in pages, and the indication is clear, namely the well-known fact that he ﷺ was unlettered.

The pages are described as "purified" (mutahharah), a derivative from the metaphorical purity, i.e., that its meanings have no confusion and do not contain anything misleading. This is an allusion to some of what is in the hands of the People of the Book of distortion and fancies.

The pages which the Messenger of God ﷺ recites are described as containing books, and books: the plural of kitab, which is a noun (fi'al) in the sense of "what is written." The meaning of the books being in the pages is that the pages on which the Qur'an is written contain the Qur'an, and it contains what the books of the earlier messengers included, of what is pure of distortion and falsehood. This is as God the Exalted said: ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97], and He said: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former pages﴾ [al-A'la: 18] ﴿the pages of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 19]. The Qur'an is the essence of what is in the earlier books and the collection of their fruit, so the name "books" was applied to the fruit of the books by way of the metaphor of part (majaz al-juz'iyyah).

By "the books" is meant the parts of the Qur'an or its surahs, which are in the position of books.

Al-qayyimah: the upright, i.e., firmly standing, where standing is here a metaphor for perfection and correctness; this is from representing the intelligible by the sensible, likening it to the one standing for its readiness for beneficial action. Its opposite is crookedness, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Praise be to God, who has sent down upon His servant the Book and has not made in it any crookedness, but made it straight﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], i.e., He did not place in it the deficiency of falsehood and error. So qayyimah is an intensive form of the one who stands, like sayyid for sa'id and mayyit.

The feminine form of the adjective is in consideration of its being an adjective for a plural.

This statement issues from the Jews who were in Medina and the villages around it, and the polytheists of Mecca who had not ceased to communicate with the People of the Scripture since the call to Islam appeared take it up, asking them for a clever stratagem by which they escape the blame of those who would reproach them for turning away from Islam. Likewise the polytheists around Medina from the Bedouins, such as Juhayna and Ghatafan, and some of the partisans in Mecca or Medina.

God related of the Jews that they said: ﴿Indeed God has taken our covenant that we not believe a messenger until he brings us an offering which fire consumes﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:183]; and He said concerning them: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from God, confirming what was with them, and previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, yet when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:89]. He related of the Christians, in His saying, as a report about Jesus: ﴿and a bearer of good tidings of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad. But when he came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is obvious magic"﴾ [al-Saff 61:6]. And He said concerning both groups: ﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could return you to disbelief after your belief, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:109]. He related of the polytheists in His saying: ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given like what Moses was given?"﴾ [al-Qasas 28:48], and their saying ﴿Let him bring us a sign just as the former messengers were sent﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:5].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 98, verse 1–3 (part 2 of 2):

There is no disagreement among the People of the Two Books that they were taken to covenant to await a prophet who would support the true religion. Its signs were set out as indications that would appear from his call, as in the words of the Torah in the Book of Deuteronomy: ("I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren, like unto thee, and I will put my words in his mouth"). Then its saying about him: ("But the prophet who shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who shall speak in the name of other gods, that prophet shall die. And if thou say in thine heart, How shall we know the word which the LORD hath not spoken? When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken") (Chapter 18). And the saying of the Gospel: ("And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever") i.e., his law, because the person of the prophet does not abide for ever ("Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him") (John, chapter 14, verse 16–17). And ("But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you") (John, chapter 14, verse 26).

And His saying: "And many false prophets shall arise, and shall deceive many" – i.e., after Jesus – "but he that shall endure unto the end" – i.e., remain until the ending of the world, and it is interpreted as the survival of his religion, since no one remains alive until the ending of the world – "the same shall be saved, and this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come" – i.e., the end of the world – (Matthew, chapter 24). That is, he is the Seal of the Messengers, as is clear.

The rabbis had misinterpreted the good tidings contained in their books concerning the Messenger who would follow, and they introduced signs by which they would recognize the promised Messenger ﷺ, which were fabricated illusions. Those who came after them remained waiting for those fabrications, and when they did not find them, they denied the one sent to them.

Al-bayyinah (the clear proof): the manifest argument and the sign of truthfulness. It is a noun transferred from an adjective, and it takes the feminine form because it is interpreted as "testimony" or "sign."

Perhaps the choice of this expression here is because it is the best rendering of the phrase found in the books of the People of the Book, which hovers around the meaning of "clear testimony" to every discerning person, as occurred in the Gospel of Matthew with the words ("for a witness unto all nations"). (Perhaps keeping this word here twice was for this particularity.) It was also mentioned alongside the earlier scriptures in His saying: ﴿And they say, "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?" Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133].

The apparent view is that the definite article in al-bayyinah is the "mental-knowledge" definite (al-'ahd al-dhihni), which is when what is meant is something known by its type rather than by its individual, as in their saying: "Enter the market," not meaning a specific market but whatever has the reality of a market. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"And war is only what you have known and tasted."

For this reason the scholars of rhetoric said: the noun defined by this alif-lam is in meaning indefinite; so it is as if it were said: "until there comes to them a clear proof."

It is also possible that the definiteness refers to something known to those being spoken of; i.e., the clear proof which is the bequests of their prophets, which is known to each group among them, even though they differed in imagining it and went far in their conjecture with what their fancies and fabrications dictated to them.

The word al-bayyinah was chosen because it expresses the meaning found in their discourse, and therefore we see its root repeated in many verses of the Qur'an on this theme, as in His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133]; and His saying: ﴿Then when their messengers came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is clear magic."﴾ [al-Saff: 6]; and His saying: ﴿after the truth had become clear to them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109]; and He said of the Qur'an: ﴿a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185].

The "min" in His saying "from the People of the Book" is explanatory (bayaniyyah), explaining "those who disbelieved."

He placed the People of the Book before the polytheists here, although the disbelief of the polytheists is more severe than that of the People of the Book, because the People of the Book have precedence in this matter: they are the ones who spread among the polytheists the notion that the described clear proof applies to them, and so they supported the polytheists in denying the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ with what was more solid than the trivialities of the polytheists, since the polytheists were unlettered and knew nothing of the circumstances of the messengers and the laws. When the Muhammadan call shook them, they turned to the Jews to receive from them what they could use to repel that call, especially after the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Medina.

So the primary aim of the refutation is the claim of the People of the Book, while the polytheists follow them.

Know that it is possible that the speech ends at His saying ﴿until there comes to them the clear proof﴾, so the pause is there, and His saying ﴿a messenger from God﴾ to the end is a new sentence in explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), and this is the view of al-Farra', i.e., "he is a messenger from God," meaning: because the ambiguity in "the clear proof" arouses the question of an inquirer about the description of this clear proof. It is a parenthetical clause between the sentence ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist﴾ to the end, and between the sentence ﴿And those who were given the Book did not divide except after the clear proof had come to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 4].

It is also possible that "a messenger" is an appositive to "the clear proof," so that it is a complete part of the expression "clear proof," and thus it is a report of what they claimed. The aim is to refute their excuses and to establish the proof against them, that the clear proof they were awaiting has arrived, but they do not reflect, or do not act fairly, or do not understand. God the Exalted said: ﴿But when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89].

The indefiniteness of "a messenger" is for the category intended by it, to ease what is difficult, like the indefinite in His exalted saying: ﴿for a specified number of days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184] and the saying ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. A Book sent down to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 1].

In this clarification there is a refutation of their excuses, as if it were said: "Then the clear proof has come to you," in the manner of His exalted saying: ﴿Lest you say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner." But there has come to you a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19]. And this indicates that the clear proof is the Messenger.

The style of this response is like the style of His exalted saying: ﴿And they say, "We will not believe you until you cause to gush forth for us from the earth a spring"﴾ [al-Isra': 90] ﴿Or you will have a garden of palms and grapes and cause rivers to gush forth within it in force﴾ [al-Isra': 91] ﴿Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments, as you claimed, or you bring God and the angels as a guarantee﴾ [al-Isra': 92] ﴿Or you have a house of gold or ascend into the sky. And we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book we can read." Say, "Exalted is my Lord! Was I but a human messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra': 93] ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said, "Has God sent a human as a messenger?"﴾ [al-Isra': 94].

In this there is a reminder of their error, for their books promised only the coming of a messenger with a law and a book confirming what was before him, and this falls within the saying of the Torah ("and I will put my words in his mouth").

And the saying of the Gospel ("and he will remind you of all that I have told you"), as has passed just above, and this is what His exalted saying indicated: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48], because the Torah and the Gospel described the promised prophet only as being like Moses or like Jesus, i.e., in that he is a messenger to whom God reveals a law, who conveys from God and speaks by His revelation, and whose sign is truthfulness, as has passed just above. The Proof of Islam (Hujjat al-Islam) said in al-Munqidh min al-Dalal: "The totality of virtuous character in our Prophet reached the point of miracle, and his miracles were extreme in their manifestness and abundance."

"From God" is connected to "a messenger," and he did not take the form of an annexation (idafah) so that the tanwin of "a messenger" could be realized, which conveys the magnification of this Messenger.

The clause ﴿reciting purified pages﴾ etc. is a second adjective or a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is an inclusion (idmaj) in praise of the Qur'an, since the apparent point is that the Messenger promised in their books was not described as reciting purified pages.

Recitation (al-tilawah) is repeating speech without adding to it or subtracting from it, whether it is written speech or memorized by heart. So the verb yatlu indicates that he reads to them speech whose words are not altered, which is the revelation sent down to him.

The suhuf (pages): the sheets and parchments prepared to be written upon, which may be of parchment or skin, or of rags. Calling what the Messenger recites "pages" is a metaphor by the relation of what will be (majaz bi-'alaqat al-ayulah), since he is commanded to write it down, so when he recites it, it will be pages. This metaphor is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, I see myself pressing wine﴾ [Yusuf: 36]. This is an indication that God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to write the Qur'an on pages and on what resembles pages, such as shoulder-blades of sheep, rags, and stones, and that the revelation sent down to the Messenger was called a Book in His saying: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51], for this very meaning.

The transitive use of the verb yatlu to suhuf is a well-known metonymic metaphor (majaz mursal) which has become equal to the literal sense. God the Exalted said: ﴿And you did not recite before it any book﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48]; it is in view of the recited thing being written. The Messenger ﷺ used to recite the Qur'an to them from memory and did not read it from pages, so the meaning of "reciting pages" is reciting what is written in pages, and the indication is clear, namely the well-known fact that he ﷺ was unlettered.

The pages are described as "purified" (mutahharah), a derivative from the metaphorical purity, i.e., that its meanings have no confusion and do not contain anything misleading. This is an allusion to some of what is in the hands of the People of the Book of distortion and fancies.

The pages which the Messenger of God ﷺ recites are described as containing books, and books: the plural of kitab, which is a noun (fi'al) in the sense of "what is written." The meaning of the books being in the pages is that the pages on which the Qur'an is written contain the Qur'an, and it contains what the books of the earlier messengers included, of what is pure of distortion and falsehood. This is as God the Exalted said: ﴿confirming what is before it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 97], and He said: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former pages﴾ [al-A'la: 18] ﴿the pages of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 19]. The Qur'an is the essence of what is in the earlier books and the collection of their fruit, so the name "books" was applied to the fruit of the books by way of the metaphor of part (majaz al-juz'iyyah).

By "the books" is meant the parts of the Qur'an or its surahs, which are in the position of books.

Al-qayyimah: the upright, i.e., firmly standing, where standing is here a metaphor for perfection and correctness; this is from representing the intelligible by the sensible, likening it to the one standing for its readiness for beneficial action. Its opposite is crookedness, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Praise be to God, who has sent down upon His servant the Book and has not made in it any crookedness, but made it straight﴾ [al-Kahf: 1], i.e., He did not place in it the deficiency of falsehood and error. So qayyimah is an intensive form of the one who stands, like sayyid for sa'id and mayyit.

The feminine form of the adjective is in consideration of its being an adjective for a plural.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, commentary on Surah 98, verse 4:

﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided except after the clear evidence had come to them.﴾

This is an escalation in refutation. It is a second refutation of their claim, by way of the dialectical counter-argument called *mu'aradah* (counter-objection), which means accepting the premise and the reasoning but using them to support what contradicts the established conclusion. This refutation is specific to the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians. For this reason, the verse makes the subject of *tafarraqa* (divided) explicit, saying "those who were given the Scripture" and not "they did not divide." Had it used a pronoun, it would have been possible to think that the polytheists were included among the referents of the pronoun, after the verse had already refuted their claim with the words: ﴿a messenger from God, reciting purified scrolls﴾ (98:2). The verse therefore rose to refuting their claims in a manner mixed with denial and with the testimony of what had happened in past times.

It is permissible for the *waw* to be a conjunctive *waw* connecting one refutation to another, and it is also permissible for it to be the *waw* of circumstance (*waw al-hal*).

The meaning is: how can they claim that their adherence to the religion they were upon was conditional upon the time when the clear evidence would come to them, when in fact clear evidence had come to them before the emergence of Islam, namely the clear evidence of 'Isa (peace be upon him)? So they became divided over belief in him, and from their division arose two religions: Judaism and Christianity.

The intended meaning of this second clear evidence is the coming of 'Isa (peace be upon him), for God sent him as their prophets had promised them, such as Elijah, Elisha and Isaiah. The Jews had agreed upon the prophet promised to them to renew the true religion, and they had been awaiting the Deliverer. When 'Isa came to them, they denied him. That is, one should not hope for their truthfulness in what they claim about awaiting a clear evidence after 'Isa, when they had already denied the clear evidence of 'Isa. Thus it became clear that denial and obstinacy are a known and established trait among them.

The intended meaning of *tafarruq* (division) is a division among the Children of Israel between one who denied 'Isa and one who believed in him, and only a small group of the Jews believed in him.

The word *tafarruq* was used as a metonymy (*kinaya*) for denying the clear evidence, because their division was a disagreement over accepting the clear evidence of 'Isa (peace be upon him). So *tafarruq* was used in both its literal and its metonymic sense, with the purpose of incorporating (*idmaj*) a reproach of them for disagreeing after the truth had become manifest, as in His saying: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of rivalry among themselves﴾ (3:19).

The definite article in the second mention of "the clear evidence" may be the mental reference (*'ahd dhihni*), or it may refer to a known thing among those being spoken of. It is a different clear evidence from the first. Its repetition is a case of repeating an indefinite with an indefinite like it, since what is known by the mental definite article is in the position of an indefinite, or it is a case of repeating a known definite with a definite like it. In both cases, the repeated item is not the same as the one before it.

The words of the commentators have agreed that the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided except after the clear evidence had come to them﴾ is that they did not diverge from following Islam, meaning they did not turn away from it except after Muhammad (ﷺ) had come. This is an interpretation of the word *tafarruq*, and it is a remote departure from its apparent sense. Hence it became unclear to them why the People of the Book were singled out for mention, when turning away from Islam was found among them and among the polytheists. They also took the second "clear evidence" to be the same as the first, which is the clear evidence of Muhammad (ﷺ). However, al-Fakhr (al-Razi) mentioned words that indicate disagreement with the commentators regarding the intended meaning of the division of those who were given the Scripture. After he had established the meaning in a way consistent with the words of the rest of the commentators, he went on to say things that require understanding *tafarruq* in its literal sense, and understanding the second clear evidence as having a meaning different from the first. He said: "The purpose of this verse is to console Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: do not let their division grieve you. This is not because of any weakness in the proof, but because of their obstinacy. Their predecessors were likewise; they did not divide over the matter of the calf-worship except after the clear evidence had come to them. So it is an ancient habit of theirs." This contradicts the beginning of his speech. Perhaps this view occurred to him, and something occupied him from clarifying it. This is among the things al-Fakhr left in his draft.

This is the third refutation of their evasion of following Islam, on the pretext that they will not abandon what they are upon until the clear proof (al-bayyinah) comes to them, and their claim that the clear proof has not come to them.

It is a refutation by way of *al-qawl bi-l-mujib* (lit. "saying according to the implication," an argumentative method in disputation), meaning: even if we grant that you are bound to hold fast to what you are upon and will not part from it until the clear proof comes to you, there is nothing in Islam that contradicts what your own Scripture brought. It commands what the Qur'an commands, namely the worship of Allah alone without associating partners. That is *al-hanifiyyah* (the primordial monotheistic faith), which is the religion of Abraham, with which they were bound by covenant. This is the religion of Islam, and it is what you were commanded in your own religion.

You may take the *wāw* (and) as coordinating the sentence with the sentence ﴿Nor did those who were given the Scripture divide except after clear evidence had come to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:4], and so on.

You may also take the *wāw* as introducing a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), so that the sentence is a *ḥāl* from the pronoun in His words ﴿until the clear proof came to them﴾ [al-Bayyinah 98:1]. The meaning would then be: "while the clear proof has in fact come to them, since Islam has come confirming the word of Allah the Exalted to Moses, peace be upon him: 'I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brethren, and will put My words in his mouth,' and the word of Jesus, peace be upon him: 'He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.'"

The verb in the passive voice (*umirū*, "they were commanded") conveys two meanings. First: they were commanded in their Scripture only with what Islam brought. Thus the meaning is: "They were commanded in the Torah and the Gospel only that they worship Allah, being sincere to Him, to the end of the verse," for the Torah insisted upon the Jews avoiding the worship of idols, and commanded prayer and commanded zakah with emphatic and repeated command. These are the foundations of the religion of Islam before fasting in Ramadan and the pilgrimage (Hajj) were enjoined. The Gospel did not contradict the Torah. Second: the meaning is that they were commanded in Islam only with the like of what their own Scripture commanded them. Thus they have no excuse for turning away from Islam, under either interpretation.

The deputy subject (*nāʾib fāʿil*) of *umirū* is omitted for generality, meaning: they were commanded with nothing except that they worship Allah.

The *lām* in His words ﴿that they worship Allah﴾ is the *lām* whose addition is frequent after the verb of desire (*irādah*) and the verb of command, and its mention was already made at His words ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [an-Nisāʾ 4:26] in Surat an-Nisāʾ, and His words ﴿and we were commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:71] in Surat al-Anʿām. Some grammarians called it *lām (an)*, "the *lām* of (that)."

*Al-ikhlāṣ* (sincerity) means purification and cleansing, that is, not associating anything else with Him in worship.

*Ad-dīn* means obedience, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "It is Allah I worship, sincere to Him in my religion"﴾ [az-Zumar 39:14].

*Ḥunafāʾ* is the plural of *ḥanīf*, which is a title for one who believes in Allah alone without partner. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "My Lord has guided me to a straight path, a correct religion, the creed of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not among the polytheists"﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:161].

This description emphasizes the meaning of ﴿sincere to Him in religion﴾, while reminding that this is the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him, whose praise and whose guidance the Torah is full of following.

The establishment of prayer (*iqāmat aṣ-ṣalāh*) is among the foundations of the law of the Torah, morning and evening.

The giving of zakah (*īttāʾ az-zakāh*) is obligatory in the Torah as an emphatic obligation.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿And that is the correct religion﴾ refers to what comes after the exceptive particle, since it is joined with the *lām* called *lām (an)*, the verbal-noun *lām*. So it is treated as a singular noun, meaning: "except with the worship of Allah, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakah." That is, "and what has been mentioned is the correct religion."

The phrase *dīn al-qayyimah* may be an ordinary *iḍāfah* (construct phrase), in which case *al-qayyimah* refers to something other than what *dīn* refers to, from among feminine-form nouns that *dīn* may be annexed to, meaning: "the religion of the correct community" or "the religion of the correct scriptures." This interpretation is supported by the fact that the indicator of the implied noun is present in the preceding wording. This is a binding argument against them concerning the rightness of Islam and that it is the correct religion. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So set your face toward the religion as a ḥanīf, the natural disposition of Allah upon which He created mankind. There is no altering of the creation of Allah. That is the correct religion, but most people do not know﴾ [ar-Rūm 30:30], ﴿turning back to Him, and fear Him, and establish prayer﴾ [ar-Rūm 30:31].

It may also be that the *iḍāfah* is nominal, from the annexation of a modified noun to its adjective, which is very common in usage. Its original form is *ad-dīn al-qayyim*, and the adjective is made feminine in view of *dīn* as *millah* or *sharīʿah* (both feminine). Or the *tāʾ* is for intensification of the adjective, like the *tāʾ* in *ʿallāmah* (very knowing). The result is the same. Under both interpretations, *dīn al-qayyimah* refers to the religion of Islam.

*Al-qayyimah* means the one most firmly upright, which has been discussed earlier.

Thus the meaning is: that which has been mentioned is the religion of the people of truth among the prophets and the righteous of the nations. It is the very thing that Islam brought. Allah the Exalted said concerning Abraham: ﴿Rather, he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 3:67]. And he said, concerning himself and Ishmael: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims [submitting] to You, and of our descendants a Muslim nation [submitting] to You﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:128]. He related their words, of him and Jacob: ﴿So do not die except as Muslims﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:132]. And Solomon said: ﴿And we were Muslims﴾ [an-Naml 27:42].

The demonstrative *dhālika* (that) refers to what they were commanded: the whole of what has been mentioned is the religion of Islam. The purpose is to establish the proof against the People of the Scripture and against the polytheists who follow them, in that they turned away from what they themselves were seeking.
