Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 98, verse 6:

(﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists will be in the Fire of Hell, abiding therein eternally. They are the worst of creation.﴾)

After he had addressed the People of the Scripture and the polytheists together, then singled out the People of the Scripture for criticism of their pretexts and for refuting their doubts, which the polytheists follow them in, he followed this with a threat against both groups, combining them as the combination between them began at the start of the surah. This is because what preceded of admonition and proof is sufficient to subdue their souls to admonition.

So the sentence is an initial resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i). He placed the People of the Scripture before the polytheists in the threat, following their being placed before them in its cause, as preceded at the beginning of the surah, and because most of the rebuttal was directed at their conditions in His saying: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not become divided until after there came to them clear evidence﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 4] up to His saying: "the upright religion," and because if the People of the Scripture had believed, the proof would have been established against the polytheists.

The "min" (من) is explicative (bayaniyyah), like the one in His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture and the polytheists were not [going to desist]﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1].

The emphasis of the predicate with "inna" (إنّ) is a rebuttal of the People of the Scripture who claim that the Fire will not touch them except for a few numbered days. The adverbial sense required by "fi" (في) indicates that they will not be removed from it, and this is confirmed by His saying: "abiding therein." As for the polytheists, they denied the recompense outright.

The statement about them being "in the Fire of Hell" is a report about what will occur in the future, by the context of threat, since threat, like promise, relates to the future. Although the nominal sentence not restricted by something specifying the time of its occurrence normally indicates that its content is happening in the present, as when you say: "Zayd is in bliss."

The clause ﴿They are the worst of creation﴾ is like a conclusion from their being in the Fire of Hell, abiding therein; therefore it is separated from the clause before it. It is a report of their evil end in the Hereafter. By "creation" (al-bariyyah) here is meant the creation commonly understood in usage, namely mankind, so there is no consideration of the devils in this name, and this resembles the customary totality (al-istighraq al-'urfi).

Al-bariyyah is on the pattern fa'ilah from bara'a Allah al-khalq, i.e., He formed the creation.

The meaning of their being ﴿the worst of creation﴾ is that they are the most evil of people. So "sharr" here is a superlative (af'al al-tafdil), its origin being "asharr," like "khayr" which means "akhyar." The attribution of "sharr" to "al-bariyyah" is according to the intention of the comparative "min."

They were like this because they went astray after being endowed with the means of guidance. As for the People of the Scripture, it is because they had a Book containing guidance and light, yet they turned away from it. As for the polytheists, it is because they were upon the hanifiyyah, then they introduced into it the worship of idols. Then they persisted in their religion after witnessing the signs of the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ and what the Qur'an brought of miraculousness and of reports about what is in the books of the People of the Scripture, which is something no one else shared with them. Thus they gathered evil for themselves, though they were fit to attain good. Therefore their regret over themselves on the Day of Resurrection is greater than the regret of others, so the two groups were worse than the idolaters and the heretics in deserving punishment, though not in what is hoped for from them of drawing near.

The demonstrative pronoun was inserted between the subject of "inna" and its predicate, to alert that they are deserving of the ruling that follows the demonstrative, on account of the qualities that precede the demonstrative, as in His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5]. The placing of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl) is to convey their exclusivity in being the worst of creation, which no other group of disbelievers shares with them, as you have learned just now. And it is not objected that the devils are worse than them, because you have learned that the name "al-bariyyah" is considered as applying to mankind.

As for "al-bariyyah": Nafi' alone read it, and Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir, with a hamzah after the yā'. It is fa'ilah from bara'a Allah, when He created.

The remaining ten readers read it with a shaddah-ed yā' without hamzah, by softening the hamzah after the kasrah into a yā', and assimilating the first yā' into the second for lightness.

Retaining the hamzah is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and the softening is the dialect of the rest of the Arabs, just as they dropped the hamzah in "al-dariyyah" and "al-nabiyy." Sibawayh said: "There is none of the Arabs but who says: 'Musaylimah prophesied' with the hamzah." However, they dropped the hamzah in "al-nabi'," as they dropped it in "al-dariyyah" and "al-bariyyah," except the people of Makkah, for they pronounce it with the hamzah and differ from the Arabs in that.

[p. 485]

(﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—they are the best of creation.﴾ ﴿Their reward with their Lord is gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him.﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 8].

The state of the disbelievers among the People of the Book and of the polytheists is set against the state of those who believe, after reference was made to them with His words: ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 5]. This covers the conditions of the groups in this world and the Hereafter, and follows the Qur'an's customary practice of pairing the warning of those who are warned with the glad tidings for those who are at peace, together with the praise that results from that. He placed the praise of them before their glad tidings, contrary to the order of the preceding speech about their opposites, so that the mention of their promised reward would be like thanks to them for their faith and their deeds, for Allah is All-Appreciative (Shakur).

The sentence is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani) arising from the repeated mention of those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists. That repetition stirs in the souls of those among the People of the Book and the polytheists who believed a question about their condition: perhaps the delay of their faith until after the revelation of the verses denouncing them places them in a lower rank. So this verse came to clarify that whoever among them believed is counted among the best of creation.

What is said about the demonstrative (ism al-ishara), the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), the restrictive particle (al-qasr), and the hamzah in (al-bariyyah) is the same as what was said about its counterpart earlier.

The demonstrative and the clause that predicates about it are, all together, the predicate of (inna).

The clause ﴿Their reward with their Lord is gardens of perpetual residence﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 8] through to its end explains the clause ﴿they are the best of creation﴾.

The phrase ﴿with their Lord﴾ is an adverbial phrase that falls as a parenthetical insertion between (jaza'uhum, their reward) and (jannatu 'adn, gardens of perpetual residence), to highlight the greatness of the reward by stating that it is stored up for them with their Lord, as an honour for them, because of what the word (ʿinda, with) carries of an indication of favour and special care, and what the expression (Rabbihim, their Lord) carries of an indication of abundant reward suited to the greatness of what it is attributed to (ʿinda), and suited to the dignity of One who nurtures (rabb), who brings His nurtured one to great beneficence.

The attribution of (jannat, gardens) to (ʿadn, perpetual residence) serves to convey that these are their dwelling place, because ʿadn means settled residence. That is, their reward is not merely a leisurely stroll through the gardens, but something stronger than that: residence in them.

[p. 486]

His words ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 8] are glad tidings that they are their enduring dwelling place.

The description of the gardens as ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 8] is to explain the utmost of their beauty.

The flowing of the river is a metaphor for the passage of water in a flood, likening the swiftness of the water's movement to the swiftness of walking.

The (nahr, river) is a great trench in the earth in which water flows, so it is not applied except to the trench together with its water. The attribution of flowing to the rivers is a broadening of speech, since what actually flows is their water, and that is what is essential to the reality of a river.

The reward of the group is expressed in the plural (gardens), and this may be distributive (tawzi'), meaning that each one has a garden, like His words: ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 19], and your saying: "The people rode their animals." It may also be that each individual has multiple gardens, and bounty does not run out. He, exalted, said: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ [Ar-Rahman: 46].

The clause ﴿Allah is pleased with them﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 8] is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (khalidin, abiding), meaning: abiding in a dwelling that coincides with Allah's being pleased with them. So during the period of their abiding in it, they are surrounded by the effects of Allah's pleasure with them, and that is the greatest of the ranks of honour. He, exalted, said: ﴿And the pleasure of Allah is greater﴾ [At-Tawbah: 72]. Allah's pleasure is the connection of His beneficence and honouring to His servant.

As for the pleasure in His words ﴿and they are pleased with Him﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 8], it is a metonymy (kinayah) for their having received from Allah's beneficence what leaves no further aim beyond it, like the words of Abu Bakr in the hadith of the cave: "So he drank until I was satisfied." And the words of Makhramah when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave him a qaba' (robe): "Makhramah is pleased." What adds to its good effect here is the verbal correspondence (musha-kalah) it contains.

**[p. 487]**

This is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*, a closing phrase that sums up the preceding matter) that follows the promise made to those who believed and the warning given to those who disbelieved. It states the cause of the reward and the cause of the deprivation, which is fear of God (*khashyat Allah*), both by what the relative clause explicitly states and by what it implies.

The demonstrative "that" refers to the reward mentioned in His words ﴿Their reward with their Lord is...﴾. The meaning is that the cause which earned them that reward is their fear of God. When they feared God, they dreaded His anger if they did not heed the one who said to them, "I am the Messenger of God to you." So they turned to considering the evidences for the Messenger's truthfulness, were guided, and believed. As for those who preferred the pleasures of this world, they turned away from the call of a messenger sent by God and did not dread the anger of the One who sent him, so they remained in their error.

Thus, the one who "feared his Lord" refers to the believers. The *lam* is the *lam* of ownership (*lam al-milk*), meaning that the reward belongs to the believers who feared their Lord. Since it is theirs, none of it belongs to anyone else. This implies the deprivation of the disbelievers mentioned earlier, and the concluding statement is complete.

Mentioning "the Lord" (*al-Rabb*) here, rather than saying "for whoever fears God" (*Allah*), carries an implicit rebuke: the disbelievers did not honour the right of lordship (*al-rububiyyah*) when they did not fear their Lord, and so they are servants of evil.

**Surat al-Zalzalah**

This surah was called, in the speech of the Companions, "the surah of *Idha zulzilat*" (﴿When the earth is shaken﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1]). Al-Wahidi related in *Asbab al-Nuzul* from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr: "It was revealed, *Idha zulzilat*, while Abu Bakr was sitting, and he wept..." (the hadith) (1). In the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, traced to the Prophet, in al-Tirmidhi: "﴿When the earth is shaken﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1] is equal to half the Qur'an." Likewise, al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi titled it thus.

It is called "Surat al-Zilzal" in many copies of the Qur'an and in many books of tafsir.

In an old Kufic-script copy from the Qayrawan manuscripts, it is called "Zulzilat." Al-Suyuti likewise named it thus in *al-Itqan*, in the section on surahs whose place of revelation is disputed. Ibn 'Atiyyah's tafsir also names it thus. However, in *al-Itqan* he did not count it among the surahs with more than one name, as if he did not regard these as names for it, but rather as quotations of some of its words. Yet naming it "Surat al-Zalzalah" is a naming by meaning, not by quoting some of its words.

Its place of revelation is disputed. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, 'Ata' and al-Dahhak said it is Meccan. Qatadah and Muqatil said it is Medinan, and this is also attributed to Ibn 'Abbas. The more correct view is that it is Meccan, and al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Naysaburi confined themselves to this view in their tafsirs. al-Qurtubi reported from Jabir that it is Meccan, and perhaps he means Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah the Companion, because what is known from Jabir ibn Zayd is that it is Medinan, for it is counted among the Medinan surahs in the order of revelation reported from Jabir ibn Zayd. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Its last verse is ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 7], revealed concerning two men who were in Medina." End of quotation. You will learn that there is no indication of this in it.

**[p. 490]**

It is counted as the ninety-fourth in the order of revelation of surahs, as reported from Jabir ibn Zayd, and al-Ja'bari versified it. This is based on its being Medinan. He placed it after Surat al-Nisa' and before Surat al-Hadid.

The number of its verses is nine according to the majority of those who count verses. The people of Kufa counted it as eight, because of the disagreement over whether His words ﴿On that day people will issue forth in scattered groups to be shown their deeds﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 6] are two verses or one verse.

The affirmation of the Resurrection, the mention of its signs, and the terror that afflicts people when it occurs. The gathering of people for the Judgment and their recompense for their deeds, whether good or evil. This is an exhortation to doing good and avoiding evil.
